title: All night on the mountain (Luke 6:1–16)
hook: before choosing the twelve, he prays all night

segments.voice: Yesterday, Levi's feast and the new wineskins. Your line was new wine takes time. Did your tiny new habit get its first day? Day five hundred twenty-two.

How do you make a decision that will shape the rest of your life? A job, a move, a marriage, who to trust. Some people make lists. Some ask friends. Some lie awake at three in the morning, scrolling. Luke shows how Jesus made one such choice: picking the small group who would carry his work after him. The chapter starts with arguments: his disciples picking grain on the sabbath, a man with a withered hand healed in a synagogue, and tempers rising over what the sabbath is for. Jesus asks: is it lawful on the sabbath to do good, or to do evil? And then, before the choice, he leaves the noise behind and climbs.
screen: `HOW DO YOU MAKE A BIG CHOICE?`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." All night. Not a quick word before bed. Hours in the dark, on a hillside, alone. Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer. He prays at his baptism. He slips away to lonely places to pray. He'll pray before Peter names him the Christ, and on another mountain before his face changes. In Luke, prayer keeps turning up at the turning points. Then: "And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles." The Greek word is apostolos, someone sent out, an envoy. Twelve, and many readers hear an echo of the twelve tribes of Israel. And Luke gives the names: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon called the Zealot; Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot. And at the end of the list, a short phrase: Judas Iscariot, "which also was the traitor." A whole night of prayer, and the list still includes the man who will betray him. Luke doesn't explain that, and doesn't try. What the text does show is this: praying first didn't guarantee an easy outcome. In Luke's telling, the choice was made in prayer, eyes open, at dawn.
screen: `JUDAS TOO, AFTER A NIGHT OF PRAYER.`
then, large: `HE CONTINUED ALL NIGHT IN PRAYER TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a big choice before you make it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a decision in front of you, big or medium. Don't solve it. Don't run the pros and cons again. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a stone in your hand, feeling its weight. Notice what you're afraid of. Notice what you're hoping for. Let the quiet do some of the work that the lists can't. If you pray, you can bring the choice to God without asking for an answer yet. If you don't, simply hold it in silence and see what rises. The bell holds the time.
Apostolos, Greek for one who is sent out, an envoy: the name Jesus gives the twelve, chosen at dawn after he prayed through the night alone on a hillside.
Your line: pray first. Before the next real decision you make today, stop for one minute of quiet first. Then choose. Day five hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Christians often pray before major decisions, and some keep a night or a day of prayer before an important choice, remembering Jesus' night on the mountain.

original.note: Greek: one who is sent out, an envoy. the name Jesus gives the twelve.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus just picked twelve friends.
what it means: Luke says he prayed through the night first, and the choice came at dawn, Judas included.
what a scholar hears: Luke's list names "Judas the brother of James," where Mark and Matthew have Thaddaeus; tradition takes them as one person.
recall: friend of God, or loved by God

sources.quoted: And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.

notes: Sabbath controversies (6:1–11) summarized briefly and without casting Pharisees as the foil; the question in the hook paraphrases 6:9.
'Luke notices Jesus praying more than any other Gospel writer' is a common scholarly observation. Confirm.
Identification of 'Judas the brother (or son) of James' with Thaddaeus is traditional; the Greek says only 'Judas of James'. Confirm phrasing.
Simon 'called the Zealot': KJV has 'Zelotes'. Paraphrased.
Reviewer edit: 'Twelve, like the twelve tribes' softened to 'many readers hear an echo of the twelve tribes' (Luke 22:30 supports the link, but 6:13 does not state it).
Reviewer edit: 'It meant the choice was made with God' softened to 'In Luke's telling, the choice was made in prayer', so the script describes the text rather than asserting a theological conclusion.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'most of us', 'his biggest choice', the comparative claim that Luke shows Jesus praying more than any other Gospel (and its myth item), the etymology framing, and the stock lines 'a phrase that stops you' and 'Christians have puzzled over it ever since'; the practice no longer opens by telling the listener to pray.
